scenarios.objective: Balance puck awareness with an off-puck threat near the net.
scenarios.briefing: Gold 1 controls the puck at the puck-side half wall. Gold 2 waits across the low slot. YOU are the weak-side defender and the coach has assigned you to stay aware of Gold 2 while D1 pressures the puck. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: Which opponent is the assigned off-puck threat?
questions.explanation: The briefing names Gold 2 as your off-puck responsibility.

questions.prompt: Select two things to keep in view.

options.text: Only the puck until a pass is made

questions.explanation: Seeing both may require repeated head checks; watching one permanently is not enough.

questions.prompt: Arrange one weak-side checking routine.

options.text: Check the puck and possible pass

questions.explanation: Checks repeat as the situation moves. The routine does not prescribe a single coverage system.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a net-side position near the low slot.
questions.explanation: This example is closer to the net than Gold 2 while offering a view of the puck. Other positions depend on your team’s coverage.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 moves higher into the slot, what should you do?

options.text: Keep marking the empty spot Gold 2 left
Chase the half-wall puck without checking

questions.explanation: The assignment concerns a changing threat, not a permanent painted spot.

questions.prompt: Describe a way to check the half wall without forgetting the low-slot threat.
questions.explanation: Mention repeated scans, body orientation or communication with D1; avoid claiming you can see everything continuously.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call while D1 pressures Gold 1 on the wall?

options.text: Gold 2 is in the low slot

questions.explanation: Calling Gold 2’s low-slot location keeps the off-puck threat in the switch conversation while D1 pressures; if Gold 2 moves higher, update the coverage lane.

questions.prompt: Which two checks let YOU support without puck-chasing?

options.text: Whether YOU should follow D1’s pressure and leave Gold 2 to the goalie

questions.explanation: The off-puck threat and D1’s pressure define your coverage lane; staring only at puck can lose Gold 2.

questions.prompt: Move YOU between Gold 2 and the Navy net while keeping Gold 1’s wall side visible.
questions.explanation: The net-side spot protects the low slot and leaves a glance toward the puck; if Gold 2 rises, follow the new lane.

questions.prompt: How can you check the puck side without abandoning Gold 2?
questions.explanation: Keep Gold 2 between you and the net, then shoulder-check the carrier and D1; if Gold 2 cuts behind, net-side coverage takes priority.

scenarios.title: Recover through useful middle ice
scenarios.objective: Choose a recovery relationship to an inside attacking threat.
scenarios.briefing: Gold 1 carries toward the Navy net near the side boards. Gold 2 is the inside support player. YOU are recovering behind the rush; D1 is already between Gold 1 and the net. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 2 is in the middle of the ice while Gold 1 is wide near the side boards.
Gold 1 carries toward the Navy net near the side boards. Gold 2 is the inside support player. YOU are recovering behind the rush; D1 is already between Gold 1 and the net.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is the inside support option?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 is in the middle of the ice while Gold 1 is wide near the side boards.

questions.prompt: What two reads could make your recovery useful?

options.text: How to chase exactly behind Gold 1 regardless of support

questions.explanation: Recovery should complement the defender and account for the inside option.

questions.prompt: Arrange one recovery decision.

options.text: Recover toward a useful net-side relationship

questions.explanation: The reference routine does not prove YOU can win a race from this still picture.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate recovery through the middle toward Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example moves toward inside danger rather than duplicating D1’s wide pressure. Whether it is reachable needs timing evidence.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 receives the pass before you arrive, what changes?

options.text: Gold 1 remains the puck carrier automatically
Your route no longer depends on the puck
Gold 2 becomes the puck threat to read

questions.explanation: The recovery job updates with possession; communicate with D1 about the new carrier.

questions.prompt: How would you know you are helping D1 rather than duplicating D1’s job?
questions.explanation: Describe coverage of another threat or lane while retaining awareness of the carrier.

questions.prompt: Which Navy defender already has the carrier-side job while YOU protects the inside route?
questions.explanation: D1 is already between Gold 1 and the Navy net, so YOU can protect Gold 2’s inside support; if D1 loses the carrier route, communicate before switching.

questions.prompt: Which two facts shape your useful recovery?

options.text: D1 already sits between Gold 1 and the net
Whether Gold 1 is the only threat because D1 has the carrier

questions.explanation: D1’s coverage and Gold 2’s inside route divide the jobs; a puck-only chase duplicates D1.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into the middle lane below Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The middle position protects the inside route and leaves D1 to manage Gold 1; if Gold 2 receives, close that carrier.

questions.prompt: How would you know you are helping D1 rather than skating into D1’s job?
questions.explanation: Cover the inside support while D1 faces the wide carrier, then communicate the handoff; if D1 loses the route, switch to the nearest danger.

scenarios.title: Locate the rebound before deciding
scenarios.objective: Distinguish a loose puck from controlled possession after a save.
scenarios.briefing: The goalie has just made a save. The rebound is loose near the side of the crease nearest the loose puck. YOU defend nearby; Gold 1 is also approaching it. The exercise starts before either player gains control. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The loose-puck marker has no owner, and the briefing says neither approaching player has control.

questions.prompt: Who controls the rebound in this setup?
questions.explanation: The loose-puck marker has no owner, and the briefing says neither approaching player has control.

questions.prompt: Which two cues matter before your next action?

options.text: The assumption that every save ends the play

questions.explanation: A save can leave a new contest; nearby opponents and the goalie also affect the response.

questions.prompt: Arrange one rebound assessment.

options.text: Check the immediate opponent and goalie
Choose a controlled next action if you can reach it

questions.explanation: The order is a suggested awareness routine, not a prescribed physical clearance technique.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward an example position near the rebound while staying net-side of Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The reference illustrates the puck-threat relationship. It does not prove safe reach or authorize contact with the goalie.

questions.prompt: The goalie now visibly covers the puck. What should you reassess?

options.text: A pass that assumes YOU already have possession
Whether further pursuit is still appropriate
A need to keep jabbing at the covered puck

questions.explanation: A visible cover changes the play. Follow the official’s signal and the competition’s rules.

questions.prompt: Why should feedback distinguish a loose rebound from a puck already controlled?
questions.explanation: Different ownership produces different choices; proximity alone is not control.

questions.prompt: What has the goalie done immediately before this freeze?

options.text: Made a save that produced a loose rebound

questions.explanation: The save creates a loose rebound and neither player controls it; if the goalie covers it later, the contest ends.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should guide your next move?

options.text: Assuming YOU owns it because you defend

questions.explanation: Puck location and opponent route decide retrieval or containment; defensive role alone does not establish possession.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a net-side angle that reaches the rebound without losing Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The offset position keeps the puck and Gold 1 in view, letting YOU contest or contain; if Gold 1 arrives first, protect the net.

questions.prompt: Why should you locate the rebound before choosing a role?
questions.explanation: A loose puck can move the next touch and ownership, so location comes before retrieval or coverage; if it is controlled, the role changes immediately.

Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 1 is a gold player and the setup assigns the puck to Gold 1.

questions.prompt: Which team has possession after the interception?

questions.prompt: Which two new concerns follow from this change?

options.text: The space toward the Navy net
Only completing the original attacking route

questions.explanation: A possession switch changes the direction of danger and the support job.

questions.prompt: Arrange one response to the turnover.

options.text: Recover or pressure according to available support

questions.explanation: This is a suggested role-change routine; exact pressure responsibilities depend on the team plan.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a position that helps against the new attack.
questions.explanation: This reference moves toward the new direction of danger and Gold 2’s side. Other recovery or pressure routes may be viable.

questions.prompt: If D1 wins the puck back, what should happen to your read?

options.text: Recheck whether an attacking outlet is available
Continue treating Gold 1 as the owner
Stop looking because the first turnover is over

questions.prompt: Name one old attacking intention you would reconsider after Gold 1’s interception.
questions.explanation: Examples include an automatic net drive or a forward support route that leaves you unable to help defensively.

questions.prompt: Which Gold player is available toward Navy’s net after the interception?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 is the available Gold support toward Navy’s net, so YOU must include that lane in the turnover read; if the carrier turns away, follow the new route rather than the first picture.

questions.prompt: Which two lanes must YOU update?

options.text: F1’s old attacking route remains the priority even though Gold now carries

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a middle cover position between Gold 2 and the Navy net.

questions.prompt: What should your first call be after the interception, and why?
questions.explanation: Call the turnover and identify the nearest lanes so teammates abandon the old attack and cover; if Navy recovers, call the new outlet.

cues: Gold 2 is central in the defending zone, nearer the slot than either wall.
